newsitem.title: USA: USDA to OK yogurt as meat replacement in schools.
newsitem.headline: USDA to OK yogurt as meat replacement in schools.

text.p: The Agriculture Department this week is going to officially allow schools to substitute yogurt for meat in their school lunch programs that feed 25 million youngsters throughout the nation, USDA officials said.

School lunch officials and nutritionists welcomed the news, and said this would give more flexibility to school lunch planners and offer non-meat eating and non-milk drinking kids a high protein and calcium option, while still being low in fat and sodium.

"Our members are very pleased," said Tami Cline of the American School Food Service Association. "It will not necessarily convert kids eating meat into eating yogurt, but we feel it will draw customers into the school cafeteria."
Under the new rules, four ounces of yogurt would substitute for one ounce of red meat. An individual-size container of yogurt is generally eight ounces.

The USDA currently purchases beef, chicken and turkey for schools to use in their feeding programs, and this year has provided schools with almost 150 million pounds of beef. USDA officials said it was unlikely the agency will buy yogurt due to its perishability, and said the local schools will probably be in charge of making those purchases.

Meat industry officials have opposed the new rule and said they were disappointed in the department's decision, but predicted only minimal impact on meat usage in school lunches because of yogurt's higher cost.

"The cost of yogurt is considerably higher than meat, so this will probably discourage schools from regularly serving it as a meat replacement," said Alisa Harrison of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association.
But others said that the convenience of yogurt and the need for much less labor preparation time than in meat will offset much of the higher purchase costs.
The Agriculture Department's acting under secretary for Food Nutrition and Consumer Services alerted a group of school nutritionists on Sunday of the agency's plan.

Speaking to the American School Food Service Association, Mary Ann Keeffe said, "Besides improving flexibility, we believe that adding yogurt will provide meal planners with another useful tool to help lower the fat content of meals."
Yogurt eating among young people in the United States has jumped dramatically in the past few years.

According to statistics from General Mills, maker of Yoplait and Colombo yogurts which account for about 27 percent of the market, the volume of yogurt eaten by children and teens has more than tripled in the last five years.
Young children and teens now account for more than a third of all yogurt consumers, said Joe Rutledge of General Mills.
Dannon yogurt, made by Dannon Co in Tarrytown, New York, is the biggest selling yogurt in the country, claiming 32 percent of the market.
